opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd point to a few big shifts.

The first is that the center of gravity is moving from training to inference. For a while, the conversation was all about who could assemble the biggest cluster to train the biggest model. That still matters, but once models are deployed to millions of users, the ongoing cost of serving them dominates. Inference is a continuous expense, so efficiency there translates directly into whether a product is economically viable.

The second is that the workloads themselves are changing shape. It used to be roughly one prompt in and one answer out. Now we see agents making dozens of calls in a loop, long-context applications, reasoning models that generate thousands of tokens before answering, and multimodal inputs. Those patterns stress systems differently. Things like reusing cached computation across requests, smarter scheduling, and handling very long sequences have gone from nice-to-have optimizations to core requirements.

Third, there's a lot more co-design between the model, the software stack, and the hardware. You can't treat them as separate layers anymore. Model architects are thinking about serving costs when they choose attention variants or mixture-of-experts designs, and systems people are building around those choices. On the hardware side, we're seeing more diversity beyond a single dominant vendor, which pushes the software layer to be more portable.

Fourth, open source has become a real force in infrastructure. Open-weight models have gotten very competitive, and open serving frameworks let companies run them on their own terms. That lowers the barrier for startups and enterprises who don't want to depend entirely on a closed API.

And finally, cost per token keeps falling quickly, which sounds like it would shrink the market, but in practice it does the opposite. When something gets cheaper, people find many more uses for it. So I think we're still early, and the infrastructure that makes AI cheaper, faster, and more reliable will be where a lot of the value gets created over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says inference is gaining importance because models serve many users and serving costs dominate, but it does not identify increasing AI usefulness as a driver of the shift.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention companies customizing AI with their own data or connect that demand to reinforcement learning commercialization.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say there are three big trends I keep coming back to.

The first is that inference has become the center of gravity. For a long time the infrastructure conversation was all about training, about who could assemble the biggest cluster. But now the dominant cost for most companies is serving models, not training them. Every time a model gets cheaper to run, people find new ways to use more of it: longer contexts, agents that make dozens of calls per task, reasoning models that generate a lot of tokens before they answer. So demand keeps outpacing the efficiency gains, and the serving stack, from the kernels up through scheduling and caching, is where a lot of the real engineering work is happening.

The second trend is that the stack is getting more heterogeneous. It's no longer just one vendor's GPUs with one software ecosystem. You have multiple hardware vendors, custom accelerators from the big cloud providers, and a lot of pressure to run the same model efficiently across all of them. That makes the software layer in the middle much more important. Open-source serving engines, compilers, and attention kernels have become the place where portability and performance actually get decided, and I think that's healthy for the market.

The third is the shift from models to systems. The thing people deploy is increasingly an agent or a pipeline, not a single model call. That changes what "infrastructure" means. You care about things like prefix caching across many turns, structured output, tool calling latency, and how to schedule thousands of concurrent long-running sessions. The workload looks very different from a chatbot answering one question at a time, and the infrastructure has to adapt.

If I had to summarize it in one line: the bottleneck has moved from "can we build the model" to "can we serve it cheaply, reliably, and on whatever hardware we happen to have." That's where I see most of the interesting work and most of the competition right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference replacing training as the infrastructure focus and links growing use cases—such as agents, longer contexts, and reasoning—to rising serving demand and engineering investment.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify companies customizing AI with their own data or connect that demand to reinforcement learning commercialization.

astra-6.text:
I’d highlight three trends. First, the focus is expanding from training models to serving them. Training is still important, but as more AI products reach users, inference cost, latency, and reliability become central infrastructure questions.

Second, the hardware and software need to be optimized together. It’s not just about buying more GPUs. How you manage memory, batch requests, and distribute workloads can make a big difference in how much useful work you get from that hardware.

Third, workloads are becoming more diverse. A short chatbot response, a long reasoning task, and a multimodal application have very different requirements. That creates room for more specialized infrastructure, while also increasing demand for tools that make those choices easier for developers.

The underlying shift is toward measuring infrastructure by the cost and quality of the application it supports, rather than simply by how much compute it provides.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame it around three shifts. First, from training to inference: as more AI products move into everyday use, infrastructure has to support ongoing demand with low latency and predictable costs. That changes how you think about compute, memory, networking, and utilization.

Second, the bottleneck is increasingly the whole system. Having powerful chips matters, but you also need to move data efficiently, keep those chips busy, and supply enough power and cooling. The opportunity extends across the infrastructure stack.

Third, workloads are becoming more diverse. A large model doing complex reasoning has different requirements from a smaller model handling a high volume of routine requests. That creates room for different hardware, deployment models, and software optimizations.

The question I’d keep coming back to is: how much useful work can you deliver at a given cost and level of reliability? That’s what connects infrastructure investment to actual customer value.

r001.rationale: The response says infrastructure is shifting from training toward inference as AI products move into everyday use, linking broader use to increased inference demand.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention companies customizing AI with their own data or that demand driving reinforcement learning commercialization.
